headlines.title: San Leandro Unified superintendent on leave after complaints of unwanted advances
headlines.description: Longtime San Leandro Unified School District Superintendent Mike McLaughlin was placed on paid administrative leave late Tuesday amid claims he acted inappropriately with another district official during a work retreat. It is unclear when or where the retreat was, but three sources with direct knowledge of the complaints tell NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit the outing involved Superintendent McLaughlin and his directors. They say alcohol was involved, and McLaughlin made unwanted advances towards a female manager. At one point, he physically touched her, they said. According to the school district and SLUSD’s board president, multiple district employees came forward about the incident, which the board determined, if true, violated Board policies and the district’s rules of conduct. The district has hired an independent investigator. The Investigative Unit reached out to McLaughlin multiple times but has not heard back. McLaughlin has held his position as superintendent of San Leandro Unified School District for 13 years. According to his contract, his base pay is $390,352. Transparent California, a public database for government employee salaries, shows he receives other pay and benefits where his total compensation annually is $523,138. “The important thing in an investigation is to maintain neutrality,” said Maureen Clark with ThreeSixty HR. Her consulting company conducts human resources investigations. Clark is not associated with SLUSD or the ongoing investigation. She said it makes sense McLaughlin is on paid leave. “You would pay it because you don’t know yet what the facts of the situation area,” she said. In a joint statement to the Investigative Unit, SLUSD and its school board president said, “The action is the immediate result of allegations made by district employees regarding inappropriate conduct in violation of Board policies and the district’s rules of conduct… The district has also immediately initiated an independent investigation into the allegations while the superintendent is on administrative leave.” They said they couldn’t provide more details until the investigation is complete and the Board of Trustees takes appropriate action. The district’s Assistant Superintendent of Educational Services Donal Patel will be serving as acting superintendent during McLaughlin’s absence.

headlines.title: Investigation underway after human skeletal remains found in San Jose
headlines.description: Human skeletal remains were found in San Jose, authorities confirmed Wednesday. The incident was reported in the area of Santa Teresa Boulevard and Bayliss Drive in South San Jose near Tulare Hill Ecological Preserve. Police reported crews were investigating a suspicious circumstance after human skeletal remains were found in the area at 3:48 p.m. Tuesday. Southbound Santa Teresa Boulevard from Bayliss Drive to Bailey Avenue was blocked off during the investigation. Police also asked the public to avoid the area and use alternate routes. The Santa Clara County Office of the Medical Examiner also responded to the scene and has taken over the investigation, police said. No other information was immediately available. headlines.title: Neighbors surprised after seeing graffiti at the top of 12-story SF building
headlines.description: A “mural” was spray-painted at the very top of a 12-story condominium building in San Francisco. The tag stretches down almost four floors, on the side of an art deco tower on Vallejo Street; in large street art style letters, it spells “Joshua” and “Neme”. At the top, the words “We own ur city now” can be read. At the bottom, the graffiti included the words “Eo4” and “Taipei 2 the Bay”. According to a Montreal-based graffiti website called Bombing Science, Eo4 is a Taipei-based tagging group. In a published interview with one of the group’s members, who calls himself Josh or Joshua, he says the group specializes in high altitude rappel tagging. Meanwhile, neighbors of the building are surprised by the scale of the graffiti, saying it happened overnight a couple weeks ago. “I don’t know who these people are and, it’s a fast job. There’s a lot of real estate on that side. You can’t hear it somehow, in the dark as well,” SF resident Lucia Choi-Dalton said. According to San Francisco police, the tagging was reported as vandalism on Aug. 6. The manager of the building says they’re currently figuring out next steps in dealing with the massive mural. According to Supervisor Steven Sherrill’s Office, the police are currently reviewing security camera video. In a prepared statement he said, in part, “Not only are these jerks destroying property, but their actions are also shockingly dangerous.” A spokesperson for the Department of Public Works says if an inspector comes out to tag this property for the graffiti, the owners will need to remove it within 30 days. One neighbor wondered how much it would cost to paint over it. “They should ask the guys who graffitied it to paint it. They know what they’re doing,” Eric McDowell said. San Francisco police note that they’ve have arrested a few prolific taggers in recent years, including one who pleaded guilty to a felony vandalism charge.

headlines.title: Person wearing Amazon vest, at least 2 others burglarize San Jose home
headlines.description: A person dressed as an Amazon delivery driver is suspected of burglarizing a San Jose home with at least two other people Tuesday. A security camera at the home appeared to capture a person, who was wearing an Amazon delivery vest and hat and carrying a package, knock on the front door in the middle of the day. After nobody answered, the person was seen repeatedly peering into the house and apparently talking to someone inside. Less than an hour later, the same camera captured a white SUV back up to the house. Three masked people, including someone wearing the same Amazon-style vest and hat, rushed to load bags into the back of the car before driving off. “They rummaged through the house and just took a whole bunch of valuables, my mom’s purses and potentially jewelry,” Andy, who asked to not be identified further due to security seasons, said. Andy claims the thieves got inside the home through a back window and escaped with high-end handbags and jewelry. “It just seems like a normal day, you’re getting a package delivered and don’t really kind of think anything strange is going on,” Andy said. Police have launched an investigation. Amazon said it’s also looking into the incident to try to determine if the person seen in the vest is in fact employed by the company.

headlines.title: Former Meta engineer says Instagram took a ‘don't ask, don't tell' approach on kids under 13
headlines.description: A former engineering director at Meta who has testified before Congress about child safety on Instagram told jurors Wednesday at a landmark trial that the company took a “don’t ask, don’t tell” approach on kids under 13 on its platforms. During his second day of testimony, Arturo Béjar said Meta consistently prioritized profits over safety in designing its products, focusing on how often and for how long people used them, even if it was detrimental to their mental well-being. “If you step away from the product, they are not going to make any money,” he said. The trial that began Tuesday in federal court in Oakland, California, pits Meta against the states of California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey and is expected to last about six weeks. The four states were among 29 that sued the tech giant in 2023 over child safety and privacy — the other 25 will go to trial later. The company also faces lawsuits in state courts, including one underway in Tennessee. The lawsuit accuses Meta of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by knowingly and deliberately designing features that addict children to its platforms and hide these harms from the public. It also argues that Meta routinely collects data on children under 13 without their parents’ consent, in violation of federal law. Meta says users must be at least 13 years old to create an account, in line with the law, called the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA. “The attitude in particular on Instagram was ‘Don’t ask, don’t tell,’” Béjar said in response to a question about his perception of the company’s attitude towards users under 13. The company has rejected the claims and said evidence at the trial will show its commitment to safety. “You will hear over the course of this case a lot of important issues, issues like teen mental health, issues like social media, issues like how teens use social media,” Meta lawyer Paul Schmidt said Tuesday. “Those are important issues, and they’re issues where Meta believes that it has a responsibility. It has a responsibility to act on its own. It has a responsibility to try to work with teens and parents in partnership to try to address those questions.” Plaintiffs’ witness says safety was an ‘afterthought’ Béjar worked at Facebook from 2009 to 2015, attracting wide attention for his work to combat cyberbullying. He returned from 2019 to 2021 as a contractor to work on safety issues. He testified before Congress in 2023 about social media and the teen mental health crisis, saying that Meta executives, including CEO Mark Zuckerberg, knew about harms Instagram was causing but chose not to make meaningful changes to address them. In his testimony Wednesday, Béjar said employee performance reviews and compensation for those who worked on user-facing products were mostly focused on user numbers and how long they spend with those products. “In that context, safety was an afterthought,” he said. The states are seeking changes to user experiences for Facebook and Instagram as well as financial damages, which could include billions of dollars in penalties. In a written statement, the office of California’s attorney general said if Meta loses, the amount of any damages would be set by the court. “This case is about stopping Meta from offering a dangerous product to teens, and from lying to teens, families, and the public about the dangerousness of their platforms. The primary remedy under our state consumer protection law is an injunction,” the statement said. Béjar walked through Meta features he said were designed for adults and are “inherently unsafe for teenagers.” This includes video autoplay, which can mean teens see videos that may cause them harm even if they don’t click on them; as well as various counters that track how many people liked, viewed or commented on your content or how many followers you have. Child development experts have noted teenagers are more susceptible to social comparison than adults, so products that reward popularity can be more harmful to their mental health. Age verification has been criticized for not going far enough Despite Meta’s statements that it works to find kids under 13 on its platforms and ban them, Béjar testified that he found “tens of thousands” of kids under 13 on Instagram through his research. He said it was “common knowledge” at the company that such young children were on Instagram. “Meta has one of the most sophisticated infrastructures in the world to detect fake accounts,” he said. But despite that, he added, there were “no goals, no metrics” to detect and check kids’ ages who were suspected to be under 13. Over the years, Meta has introduced features it says are designed to make the experience safer for young people. But Béjar said these did not work. For instance, a tool called “Take a Break,” introduced in 2021, is a feature that is “designed to fail,” he said. First, it is a setting that people have to turn on if they want to use it. Béjar said that in his experience building settings, very few users actually go through the trouble of turning them on. He compared it to an airbag that drivers have to turn on every time they get in a car. “A safety tool has to be on by default,” he said. The feature can also be dismissed with a tap of a finger. If Meta was serious about wanting users to take a break, Béjar said, it would not be so easily swiped away. ___ AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed to this story from Los Angeles.

headlines.title: José Suárez, former Telemundo Sacramento and Fresno GM, killed in helicopter crash
headlines.description: The Latino community in Northern California mourns the death of former Telemundo Sacramento and Fresno General Manager José Alberto Suárez, who was one of the Americans flying in a helicopter that crashed in Samburu County, Kenya. Suárez served as the president and general manager of Telemundo 33 Sacramento and Telemundo 51 Fresno from April 2019 until February 2024, when he went back to his home state of Florida to manage the Orlando, Tampa and Fort Myers stations. His legacy in Northern California “José Alberto Suárez was a visionary, someone who united people, a mentor and a tireless advocate for our Latino community,” Telemundo’s Sacramento and Fresno stations said in a joint statement. “José had an extraordinary capacity to bring people together, not simply around an event or an initiative, but around a shared conviction: that when we work together, we can strengthen our communities.” A track record spanning more than two decades With more than 25 years of experience in media, Suárez also served as president at other stations, including Telemundo Las Vegas, Telemundo Utah and Telemundo San Antonio. Some of his career accolades include receiving a Lone Star Emmy, a Suncoast Emmy, three Best Daily Newscast Emmys, as well as several Associated Press awards. Suárez loved cars and photography, according to his X account. Telemundo will provide more information in the coming days about how they will honor Suárez’s life and legacy.

headlines.title: Wahab narrowly ahead of Hernandez in California Congressional District 14 race
headlines.description: State Sen. Aisha Wahab, D-Hayward, was narrowly leading in the early results released from Tuesday’s special election to fill the rest of the congressional term in the East Bay seat formerly represented by Eric Swalwell. Wahab had 33,399 votes, or 51%, compared to 32,043 and 49% for Melissa Hernandez, a BART board director and former Dublin mayor, according to the unofficial results released from the initial vote-by-mail ballots counted by the Alameda County Registrar of Voters. The two were in a runoff to fill the rest of Swalwell’s term that ends in January for California’s 14th Congressional District after neither garnered a majority in a June 16 special election where Wahab received 43% of the vote and Hernandez 17%. Swalwell resigned from his congressional seat in April amid accusations of sexual assault. He has denied all allegations against him. The county Registrar of Voters said more results from the election will be released on Friday, then again Aug. 26 and Aug. 28. In a race that’s seen some heated accusations on both sides, Wahab says she’s confident her political history and record with the voters gives her an edge. “I am the state senator. I have capped HOA fines at $100, capped insulin at $35 for a 30-day supply. I believe in Medicare for all, I believe in social safety nets and really pushing back on the cuts to our most vulnerable communities. And I believe in human rights for all,” Wahab said. Hernandez says she’s confident voters will see her as the candidate focused on the right issues because she’s taken the time to connect. “When I go knocking on those doors, they’re worried about groceries being too high, the gas prices being too high and also the fact that we want to be able to have our next generation, our children, their children, stay in the place they grew up in if they choose to,” Hernandez said. Political Analyst Larry Gerston says the race is also getting a lot of attention because voters are being asked who should hold the seat for a few months and then they’ll be asked to come back in November and decide whether that person should get a full two-year term. Gerston says the electorate in that November race could end up being much different from this one. “You have the activists and many other moderates coming out in November. Whoever gets the moderates is likely to prevail given what we see now, that may help Hernandez more than more than Wahab,” Gerston said. Along with Tuesday’s election to decide who fills the seat for the final months of Swalwell’s term, Wahab and Hernandez finished as the top two candidates in the June 2 primary and will face off again in November in a separate runoff for the next congressional two-year term to represent District 14, which includes the cities of Hayward, Pleasanton, Livermore, Union City, Castro Valley, and parts of Dublin and Fremont. Decision 2026 Aug 18 Decision 2026 Aug 17 California special election to fill Swalwell's Congressional District 14 seat
headlines.source: Dan McMenamin | Bay City News and Robert Handa

headlines.title: Arrest made in suspected Richmond arson that killed man, 5-year-old boy
headlines.description: A man was arrested on suspicion of murder and arson after a Richmond house fire killed a 47-year-old man and 5-year-old boy, police said, adding a woman and child were also critically hurt in the blaze. Firefighters initially responded to a separate fire on the 200 block of 15th Street at about 8:08 p.m. Tuesday. The blaze, which is also being investigated as an arson, was declared under control just before 9 p.m., and its cause remains under investigation. No one was injured. About 45 minutes after the initial response, while crews were mopping up the first fire, they noticed smoke and flames coming from a home two doors north. The second fire was upgraded to three alarms due to its significant size and the resources needed to respond to the number of victims, fire officials said. Richmond firefighters were assisted by crews from the El Cerrito Fire Department and Contra Costa County Fire Protection District. Firefighters entered the second home and found four people inside, officials said. The 47-year-old man and 5-year-old boy died as a result of the fire, while a 33-year-old woman and 2-year-old girl remained in critical condition. “This is an absolute, unimaginable tragedy,” Richmond police Chief Timothy Simmons said. “It has taken the life of a man and a young child while leaving a woman and another young child literally fighting for their lives.” Despite the location and timing of the two suspected arsons, police said they’re not related. Witnesses said the man who died was seen helping people at the scene of the first fire. “He was helping,” witness Armando Lara said. “So everything got under control. He just went back inside. When the next fire started, that was weird. Nobody screamed ‘Fire!’ They didn’t come out from the back door or anything.” Detectives with the Richmond Police Department’s homicide unit began investigating after the second fire started. During the investigation, detectives identified 32-year-old Sergio Rivera-Vega as the person suspected of intentionally setting the second home on fire, police said. Rivera-Vega is a relative of the victims and lived at the home. Police said Rivera-Vega was found near the scene and taken into custody without incident. “As our detectives were on scene, one of our detectives saw the suspect standing behind our yellow tape at the scene,” Richmond police Lt. Joseph England said. Lara, who also owns a restaurant nearby, shared video footage he said showed Rivera-Vega moments after the deadly fire broke out. Lara said the footage showed Rivera-Vega flipping over his restaurant’s bench. Lara also claimed Rivera-Vega tried to set his restaurant on fire last month. Police did not comment on that allegation. “[Rivera-Vega] was frustrated, like he know he did something wrong,” Lara said. “I feel bad for the family.” Rivera-Vega was booked into jail on two counts of murder and two counts of arson causing great bodily injury, according to police. His bail was set at $2.5 million. In the first fire, a neighbor provided surveillance video that showed a woman, believed to be a tenant, walking away from the home with a cart full of items moments before flames erupted. Police made an arrest but did not immediately provide information on the suspect. The homeowner, who did not want to be identified, believes the tenant set the fire, adding that police had been called to investigate her several times. Because both fires are considered suspicious, arson investigators, along with the Richmond Police Department and the Contra Costa County Sheriff’s Office, are investigating.

headlines.title: Dog rescued as fire damages 2 San Jose homes
headlines.description: Firefighters responded to a second-alarm residential fire involving two homes in San Jose on Wednesday, according to the San Jose Fire Department. The fire was reported on the 2000 block of Santiago Avenue. Fire officials said both homes had compromised gas meters that were fueling the flames. PG&E crews secured the gas lines, according to the fire department. Firefighters rescued one dog, and no injuries were reported. Authorities asked people to avoid the area while crews responded to the fire.

headlines.title: 9-year-old boy taken to trauma center after being hit by driver in Santa Rosa
headlines.description: A driver struck a 9-year-old boy as he was crossing a street in Santa Rosa Tuesday night, leaving him with significant injuries, police said. The collision happened at about 8:30 p.m. along the 900 block of Yulupa Avenue, according to police. The child was crossing Yulupa Avenue when he was hit by a 41-year-old Santa Rosa man driving a white Ford Mustang, police said. Investigators believe the boy was in a marked crosswalk when he was struck. They were working to determine if the crosswalk lights were activated at the time. The boy suffered significant injuries and was taken to a regional trauma center by ambulance, police said. The driver stayed at the scene and cooperated with investigators, according to police. Alcohol and drugs do not appear to have played a role in the collision. It wasn’t immediately known how fast the driver was going at the time. An investigation is underway. Anyone who witnessed the collision or has additional information is asked to email police investigator Anthony Matteri at amatteri@srcity.org.

headlines.title: Foul play suspected in Chantel Brooks' disappearance, Fairfield police say
headlines.description: Foul play may have been involved in the disappearance of Chantel Brooks, the Fairfield Police Department said in a statement Tuesday. Brooks, who turned 37 last week, was last seen on July 17 at 1:45 a.m. leaving a CVS Pharmacy store in the 300 block of East Travis Boulevard in Fairfield, where she lives. Security camera footage from Le Nain Hotel in San Francisco’s Tenderloin District, where Brooks is a desk clerk, shows her leaving work at around 12:20 a.m. that night. On August 5, Fairfield Police issued a public notice of Brooks’ disappearance and requested the family’s help. Her brothers, Kevin Robinson and Omar Hasan, said in an interview that they’ve been meeting every week with Fairfield police for updates on the case. Hasan, who lives in Reno, Nevada, has been staying with family in Vallejo during the search. “When we first heard about it, we hit the ground running,” Robinson said. “Being her brothers, we’re her first line of protection … We’re all on our knees together, praying.” Brooks, who was born and raised in San Francisco, has 13 brothers and sisters, Robinson said, as well as cousins all around the Bay Area. “Any time we get a tip, we all know about it,” said Robinson, noting that he and his siblings are communicating more than they have in years. Family members have gone door-to-door in Fairfield to ask about Brooks and learn more about her life in Fairfield. They celebrated her 37th birthday with a vigil on Thursday in Fillmore-Turk Mini Park in San Francisco, said Robinson. “She’s warm and outgoing,” Robinson said. “Everyone she meets remembers her.” To date, the investigative efforts have included dozens of search warrants, multiple coordinated ground searches involving search and rescue resources through the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services, as well as extensive aerial drone grid searches. The department is also working closely with the Solano County District Attorney’s Office while working through various leads in her disappearance. The public is urged to call the Fairfield Police Department at 707-428-7300 or email case267208@fairfield.ca.gov. Anonymous tips can be left with the department’s Investigations Division at 707-428-7600.

headlines.title: Oakland Unified receives negative credit rating outlook
headlines.description: There are new concerns about the financial health of the Oakland Unified School District after a Fitch credit rating gave the district a negative outlook for the current fiscal year. Fitch cited several factors, including ongoing fiscal pressure, the loss of unrestricted reserves and uncertainty over the district’s ability to restore fiscal stability. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that the latest Fitch rating is one notch below the district’s previous grade. The assessment comes as district leaders have recently said OUSD’s finances have significantly improved, including reaching a balanced budget. Fitch and the Chronicle are both owned by Hearst. OUSD did not provide a response.
